newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Cotton prices seen rising in Pakistan and India.
newsitem.headline: Cotton prices seen rising in Pakistan and India.

text.p: Cotton prices are likely to rise in the coming week in Pakistan and India amid rising demand for fresh crop arrivals, dealers said on Thursday.
Dealers in Karachi said Pakistani prices rose in the week to Thursday after officials forecast a drop in cotton production in the main growing Punjab province.

The state-run Pakistan Central Cotton Committee (PCCC) on Tuesday estimated the 1996/97 (July-June) crop at 9.2 to 9.5 million 375-lb bales, below a target of 10 million bales and the 1995/96 crop of 9.96 million bales.
A PCCC statement blamed pests and unfavourable weather for the reduced forecast, but stressed it was tentative and should not be taken as the final crop size.
"The next three to four weeks are crucial and could affect yield per acre either way," the statement said.
On Thursday Karachi Cotton Association spot rates, including a 10 percent sales tax, rose as spinners scrambled to cover future requirements amid the lower output forecast.

KCA spot rates for NIAB-78 variety rose 16.50 rupees ($0.44) to 2,377.50 rupees per maund (37.32 kg) and MNH-93 rose 27.50 to 2,332.50 rupees per maund. On the kerb, NIAB-78 traded in a 2,125-2,000 rupee range, dealers said.

In Bombay, Indian cotton prices bounced back in the week to Thursday on renewed mill buying ahead of Hindu festivals, traders said.
"Purchases by state-owned agencies, particularly the Cotton Corporation of India, also helped prices recover," a trader said.
Traders said the pace of arrivals in the northern states of Punjab and Haryana had improved but demand had exceeded supply.
"Farmers were bringing cotton in small quantities to the market because of depressed prices last week," one trader said.
In spot, Bengal-deshi (ready delivery) rose 150/190 rupees to 990/1,070 rupees per maund and Punjab sawginned by 60/85 rupees to 1,660/1,730 rupees.
Gujarat Kalyan gained 300/400 rupees to 12,800/13,000 rupees per candy (355.56 kg) and long-staple Gujarat Sankar-4 rose 400/500 to 20,500/21,200 rupees per candy.
"Market sentiment is firm and traders expect prices to move higher on hopes that credit controls on cotton trade will be withdrawn," an official of a textile mill said.
The Reserve Bank of India is due to announce its credit policy for commercial banks for the second half of fiscal 1996/97 (April/March) on Saturday.
